name: Carlos Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Tell me about a normal factory shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three, a junior operator on the carton folding and gluing machine in a packaging factory. I left school after secondary school and am still learning how to set the feed guides without creasing the boxes, so I check the first stack with a more experienced operator. I never use AI tools; I like a paper setup sheet I can mark. The pay is low for this work, we have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are only a few similar factories nearby. My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a computer can tidy the box orders, but the cartons still jam if the guide is wrong. Our shop needs hands that can stop the gluer before a whole stack folds badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with no big AI change, a short week would put our mortgage close to trouble. I am low paid, still learning and have less than one month saved; the few nearby factories do not give me much room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the folding-gluing line and ask the experienced operator to check my first stack each shift. I would ask our union representative to raise the unpredictable weekly hours at the next shift meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious already because ordinary lost hours could hit our mortgage. A quiet AI future does not make a thin bank account thicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which machine mistake worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a feed guide is too tight, the carton corner creases and the glue lands in the wrong place. I stop the belt and show the first bad box to the lead operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the weekly rota posted early and a minimum paid shift if they call us in. I cannot plan a mortgage payment around a text the night before.

The **union** should ask for early rotas and minimum paid call-in shifts.
think: A **missed** week could endanger the **mortgage** even without AI disruption.
**Low** pay, little savings and few local factory jobs leave me exposed.
do: **Keep** checking first folded cartons with the experienced operator.
**Ask** union representative for earlier rotas and minimum paid shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary hours and mortgage payments.
S0.quote: A quiet AI future does not make a thin bank account thicker.
fieldNote: **Carlos** is still **learning** carton guide settings and asks for a second physical check.
The **baseline** **mortgage risk** comes from low pay, less than a month saved and uncertain weekly hours.

steps.text: Keep running carton gluer and check first stack with lead operator

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our union group to look closely at an AI rota before management calls it efficient. Booking and planning may move to software first, but a carton still needs someone at the jam switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think an automatic schedule could cut my paid setup minutes or give the better shifts to the senior operators. With the mortgage and almost no reserve, even a small weekly pay loss could show up at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the folding line running and bring my last four rotas to the union meeting to ask for paid setup time. If hours are cut and a posted nearby carton-operator vacancy offers pay that covers our mortgage and bills, I would apply; I would not leave for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic cut to my own paid hours. I can bring records and look for a vacancy, but neither pays the bill this Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the four rotas show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark every paid setup minute before the first carton went through, then compare it with the new schedule. A faster printed rota cannot set a feed guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much pay must another job bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to cover the mortgage, food and the children’s school costs after travel. A farther factory at the same low rate would make us poorer.

say: The **AI rota** should not erase paid setup time on the carton line.
I would **take** **four rotas** to the union meeting.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink before robots touch the machine.
The **mortgage** and tiny reserve leave little tolerance for a smaller wage.
do: **Bring** four rotas to union meeting and request paid setup time.
**Keep** checking carton feed guides and first stacks.
**Apply** after cuts to posted nearby adequate carton role.
S1.quote: A faster printed rota cannot set a feed guide.
fieldNote: **Planning** AI reaches **rosters** before capable robots reach carton handling.

steps.text: Bring four rotas to union meeting for paid carton setup time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches ordering and rosters in 2028 when I am forty-five, then capable robots reach carton handling around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A robot that feeds and clears the gluer could replace junior hands first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose most of my paid shifts if this factory buys a capable robot. We have less than a month saved, a mortgage and two children; I lie awake working out which payment could wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a written staffing and notice plan, then call the lender to ask about a payment pause before any missed mortgage payment if robot cuts are announced. If a posted nearby warehouse or carton job pays enough for mortgage and bills, I would apply immediately; I would stop nonessential spending if shifts fell. I cannot pay for a course out of this household account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by a likely large wage loss and the nights I already spend on the mortgage. The union and lender calls buy time, but I do not know if they bridge a lost job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop buying first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The family would stop paid weekend outings before touching the children’s meals or school supplies. We have little spare spending to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI tool to find work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never used one and would start with posted vacancies and the union noticeboard. I would ask someone to show me a real opening, not send my details into a system I do not understand.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may change rosters before carton robots around 2031.
The **union** must demand written staffing notice.
think: I **expect** most **junior paid shifts** to go after robot carton handling.
**Less** than a month saved and a mortgage keep me awake.
do: **Ask** union for written staffing and notice plan.
**Apply** immediately to a posted nearby warehouse or carton job only if wages cover the mortgage and household bills.
**Cut** paid outings if robot cuts reduce shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.
S2.quote: We have less than a month saved, a mortgage and two children; I lie awake working out which payment could wait.
fieldNote: His **alarm** reflects an **expected large cut** and explicit sleeplessness, not just political anger.
He would **contact** the **lender** before arrears and apply only to a posted nearby job covering household bills.

steps.text: Ask union for written robot staffing and notice plan
Apply immediately to posted nearby warehouse or carton job only with mortgage-covering and bill-covering pay
Stop paid weekend outings if robot shifts fall
Ask mortgage lender about payment pause before arrears if robot cuts announced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that thinking AI reaches ordering in 2031 when I am forty-eight, and capable carton robots follow around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five years is enough for a proper paid training route, if management agrees to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think the junior gluer shifts could shrink, but the extra years let us reduce some mortgage debt. I have no money for unpaid study and do not trust a course unless a real job uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the carton shifts and pay an extra small amount toward the mortgage from any overtime actually worked. If the factory offers a fully funded machine-setter certificate on paid time with supervised guarded practice, and a posted nearby setter job covers our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; I would ask the union to secure those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic future loss of hours, but I have more control with paid years ahead. I am wary of screens, yet I could learn a physical setter task beside an instructor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would extra mortgage money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only overtime actually paid, after food and school costs. I would not count a hoped-for shift as money already saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does guarded practice mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trainer would stop and isolate the carton gluer before I touch a feed assembly. I would refuse a demonstration on a moving belt.

say: **2031 thinking AI** precedes carton-handling robots around 2034.
I would **ask** for a **paid setter route**, not an unpaid course.
think: The **junior hours** remain vulnerable, but five years help.
A **real** nearby adequate job must exist before I enrol.
do: **Pay** extra mortgage principal from overtime actually received.

feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts with more preparation time.
S3.quote: I would not count a hoped-for shift as money already saved.
fieldNote: He **accepts** **hands-on training** only when funded, paid, guarded and tied to a posted nearby adequate setter role.
**Extra** mortgage payment comes from **actual overtime**, not from existing savings or imagined future hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches ordering in 2036 when I am fifty-three, and capable carton robots follow around 2039 when I am fifty-six. Ten years gives my children time to finish more school, but it does not give me another wage at fifty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can become a better carton operator while I am paid, yet robots may still take the feeder work. I would need to keep the mortgage moving and see which nearby jobs really stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the gluer shifts and put any new overtime money toward extra mortgage principal after essentials. I would attend a fully funded, paid-time guarded machine-setter certificate if the plant offers a place and a posted nearby setter role pays our bills, then apply after qualifying if hours fall. I would keep pressing the union for paid training and notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about later paid-hour cuts, though the longer runway gives us more time. I still cannot buy training with a thin household reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them to finish school and learn how machines work, not assume a factory will keep the same jobs forever. Their choices are theirs, but I want them to have more than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a new AI scheduling app yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the printed rota and ask the representative to check missing hours. I have never used AI tools, and I would not pretend that reading a schedule teaches me one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most. Carton-handling robots around 2031 could take most of my junior shifts while we have less than a month saved and a mortgage. A written notice plan and a nearby job at a wage covering our bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the children when a parent loses a factory wage. I can give up an outing, but I cannot tell the mortgage lender that a robot is still being tested. The carton gluer is a machine; our home is not a spare part.

headlineQuote: The carton gluer is a machine; our home is not a spare part.
portrait: **Carlos**, **43**, is a junior carton-gluer operator with secondary schooling and a mortgage.
His **partner** and two school-age **children** depend on a low factory wage; savings cover less than a month.
He has **few nearby factory options** and never uses AI tools, preferring paper setup sheets.
He **turns** to the **union** for notice and paid guarded training, then applies only for posted work that pays the household bills.
biggestWorry: **Fast** carton-handling robots around **2031** could remove most junior shifts before his family builds even one month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing notice**, lender breathing room and posted nearby bill-covering work would help him respond.
